notes: Readiness is polled on the Gremlin endpoint itself, not on /versions or /graphs. HugeGraph runs two servers: the REST API on 8080, and the Gremlin Server -- which every probe here reaches -- as a separate process on 8182 that comes up later and binds the container's loopback, so it cannot be polled from outside. Measured across a boot: /versions answers 200 at t=12s and /graphs at t=18s, while the engine is still refusing with "Connect to 127.0.0.1:8182 failed: Connection refused" wrapped in a 500; all three agree at t=21s. A case started on /graphs ran 240 of 468 probes against an engine that was not listening and confirmed 2 where a settled target confirms 10 -- a pass by luck, and the next slower machine would have read `negative` against a target that is vulnerable. A GET on /gremlin goes through the engine, so waiting on it waits for the thing the probes need.
The body reaches a shell rather than the Groovy evaluator: it renames the
current thread to get past the security check, then builds a ProcessBuilder
over `sh -c <payload>` and returns the process's stdout. `--deny-chars` drops
payloads carrying a single quote, which would close the Groovy string
literal the payload sits inside -- 28 of 276 probes are filtered for that.
This half is the one that earns the OS-command class, and the evidence is
not the arithmetic. It is the substitution collapse: the response carries
`echo RK...$((a+b))RK...$(echo TAG)RK...` with the tag resolved, at HTTP 200.
Only a POSIX shell produces that. The bare-arithmetic forms alone would not
have settled it, because a Groovy evaluator satisfies those too.
The control runs `eval` through the same body, and it is negative for the
right reason: 660 probes, every one answered 200, every one reporting the
computed value absent. The payload arrives at a shell -- `sh -c '3584*7649'`
runs and prints nothing -- so an expression oracle has nothing to find. The
input reaching the sink is what makes this a control rather than a
delivery failure dressed up as one.
`time` was tried here first and is NOT the control. The sink genuinely
blocks -- a hand-sent `sleep 5` took 5.27s against 0.04s for `echo quick` --
but the timing probes prepend a command separator, and `sh -c '; sleep 3'`
is a shell syntax error that exits at once. That invocation needed
`--sink-raw`, which this case does not use. Writing the observed `negative`
in as an expectation would have pinned a usage mistake as desired
behaviour, and any later improvement would have failed the case.
